messages.author: 0d4085b4474fa32a
messages.subject: speeding up k-fold cross validation
parts:
Hi,
I want to estimate predictive performance by k-fold cross validation (k=10) for a bunch of models. (I tried first  PSIS-LOO, but some of the models had  khats above 1) and I was wondering how to speed up  fitting 10 times each model.  I already know that these models converge with 2000 iteration with adapt_delta=.99,max_treedepth=12,stepsize=0.01, so I guess I can run only one chain with each partition. Is it right? (This way I could  run 10 models in parallel in 10 cores). 
And my second question (which I hope is not completely stupid), can I reduce the warmup somehow by using information from the fitted models? and if so how/which information should I use?

Thanks!!
Bruno

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: speeding up k-fold cross validation
parts:
On Saturday, May 7, 2016 at 10:04:09 AM UTC+3, Bruno Nicenboim wrote:
Hi,
I want to estimate predictive performance by k-fold cross validation (k=10) for a bunch of models. (I tried first  PSIS-LOO, but some of the models had  khats above 1) and I was wondering how to speed up  fitting 10 times each model.  I already know that these models converge with 2000 iteration with adapt_delta=.99,max_treedepth=12,stepsize=0.01, so I guess I can run only one chain with each partition.

Running several chains would be better. What is the n_eff for the quantity you are interested in now? What would be the expected n_eff with one chain? Would that be large enough for your purposes? Could you manage with several shorter chains?

Is it right? (This way I could  run 10 models in parallel in 10 cores). 
And my second question (which I hope is not completely stupid), can I reduce the warmup somehow by using information from the fitted models? and if so how/which information should I use?

Since we can assume that posteriors for each fold are close to the full posterior, it would be possible to initialise the mass matrix and other adapted parameters to save time on the adaptation phase, and you could intialise parameter values using the samples from the full posterior samples, but still you could save less than 50% time. And I think it's not yet possible to skip the adaptation yet.

So my suggestion is to run several shorter chains for each cv-fold. Shorter warm-up should be enough if you initialise the parameters for each run from the full posterior samples (different values for each chain)

Aki

 

Thanks!!
Bruno

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: speeding up k-fold cross validation
parts:
Hi Bruno!

I just recently was in the same trouble to be force to refit a Stan model over and over again to almost the same data. What I figured would be to transform my parameters to unit scale and 0 centered. So from your runs you know the posterior sd and center. Parametrize your model such that everything lives on the unconstrained space. Then you can use something like this scheme:

parameter block:
vector[K_phi] phi_raw;

transformed block:
  // shift and scale such that raw parameters are 0 centered and have
  // scale 1
  phi <- location_phi + scale_phi .* phi_raw;


The location_phi and scale_phi are the posterior estimates from previous runs (take mean and sd or use robust alternatives). You can still place a prior on phi since the Jacobian is a constant here, but the variables being sample are at unit scale around 0. Since warmup is actually about finding these scales and the centers, you can then shortcut warmup dramatically. There are 3 phases during warmup (explained in the manual) - I simply shortened these to 1/4 and my warmups are now roughly 3x times as fast. I also run a sanity check in that at the end of the fit I check Rhat being below 1.2 for all stuff I care about. If this is not the case, then I rerun Stan with a longer warmup (only cut down by 1/2) and hope things are fine.

This procedure is really a big step forward for me, but it can be dangerous, of course, but should work well in your setting.

Ah, don't forget to initilize phi_raw with unit normals or better make it under-dispersed, so N(0, 1/4); albeit the correct way would be to use N(0, 2) to my understanding, but this will probably only cost you more computation time to get warmup going, so an sd of 1/4 is safer.

Sebastian
